newsitem.title: USA: U.S. still studying German Scientology move.
newsitem.headline: U.S. still studying German Scientology move.

text.p: The U.S. State Department reacted cautiously to Germany's announcement on Friday that it was placing the Church of Scientology under observation, saying it was still studying the implications of the move.

Germany's interior ministry and 16 regional states said a working group had recommended that sufficient suspicion existed of the church's anti-democratic intent to merit surveillance by anti-extremist watchdogs.
"What we need to do is study this issue, talk to the German government about it, and then perhaps we'll have something to say later on," said State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns.

Burns noted that for several years running the State Department's annual human rights report had discussed allegations by the Scientology church that German government measures violated its religious rights.
But, as in previous comments on the issue, Burns also dismissed what he called a "wild charge" by Scientology that Germany's treatment of the group could be compared to Nazi treatment of the Jews.

Scientology, based in Los Angeles, was founded in 1954 and based on the teachings of late American science fiction writer L. Ron Hubbard. Its members take personality tests and are then offered courses and literature to help them realise what the group believes is their full potential.
Germany argues that Scientology is purely an economic organisation which exploits the insecurities of its members to extract big profits from the self-improvement courses.
